messages.subject: Using git bisect
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

I've recently become a fan of using git bisect to find the sources of bugs.

Briefly, if you know that the current commit is bad, and that some previous commit is good, then you can use git bisect to find the commit that introduced the bug, using a binary search. It checks out a commit somewhere in the middle if the known good and bad commits, then you test and tell it whether the commit is good or bad; this process is repeated until you find the first bad commit. This usually makes it a lot easier to find the cause.

Testing can be automated if you write a script to run the tests. You can just start the testing and walk away, and a couple minutes later, it will report the commit that introduced the bug.

I've written up how to use git bisect with ggplot2 here:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/Using-git-bisect-to-hunt-bugs
The page also includes some example scripts for automatic testing, which should be easy to customize.

Feedback is welcomed!
-Winston

messages.body_plain:
> I was thinking that this would be taken care of at the devtools level
> - i.e. it would load the package for you, and skip if it errors on
> load.

OK, I have something that works and gives a reasonably clean interface. Here's an example of a fully-automated test script:

#/usr/bin/Rscript
cat("\n===== Running test script ======\n")
library(devtools)

# If error loading, skip this commit
bisect_load_all('.', on_error = NA)

# The test code
testRun <- function() {
  dat <- data.frame(x=1:3, y=1:3)

  # Bad: Throws error when breaks=NA
  p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() +
        scale_x_continuous(breaks=NA)
  x11()
  print(p)

  # If it reaches this point, then it successfully printed. Mark GOOD
  return(TRUE)
}

# Run the test. If error, mark BAD
bisect_test(testRun, on_error = FALSE)

And here's an example of a test function that requires interactive response (for brevity, I won't repeat the loading code at top):

# A test that requires visual inspection and manual response
testRunInteractive <- function() {
  dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:5], y=1, z=(1:5)/4)

  # Bad: Show's NA at high and low end of legend
  p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=z)) + geom_bar()

  # Need to manually open x11 window because we're in a script
  x11()
  print(p)

  # User must visually inspect and mark good/bad/skip
  bisect_return_interactive()
}

# Run the test. If error, mark SKIP
bisect_test(testRunInteractive, on_error = NA)

I've put the function definitions here -- this is the stuff that would go in devtools:
https://gist.github.com/1721649

In addition to TRUE=good, FALSE=bad, and NA=skip, I added NULL=do nothing (continue running script). I made use it when running load_all(), which returns NULL. It will also be useful if someone wants to run a two-stage test like this:
1. Setup stuff (after the load_all) - if error here, SKIP
2. The actual test - if error here, BAD

setupStuff <- function() {
  # Do some setup stuff
  return(NULL)
}
bisect_test(setupStuff, on_error = NA)
bisect_test(realTest, on_error = FALSE)

It's conceivable that there would be breakage in the setup part -- that something else broke that prevents you from getting to the important part of the test. (I've seen some really ... interesting stuff when jumping around the commit history with a bisect. Things work pretty well at the beginning (0.8.9) and at the end (0.9.0), but in the middle it gets pretty weird.)

Let me know what you think of this version (structure, function names, etc)... If it looks good, I'll add it to a branch on devtools.
-Winston

messages.body_plain:
OK, I couldn't resist trying out a bisect script on this one.

Download this script and save it in your ggplot2 directory as granova_test.r:
  https://gist.github.com/1721954
The code at the top is a set of functions that's destined to go in devtools; the interesting stuff is at the bottom.
This script installs ggplot2 from your source tree time it's run, and then runs the test with geom_rug_alt.

The script assumes that, relative to your ggplot2 directory, your granovaGG directory is at ../granovaGG. If it isn't, edit the script to correct the path.

Then, in your ggplot2 directory, run this:
chmod +x granova_test.r
git bisect reset
git bisect start master remotes/origin/ggplot-0.8.9
git bisect run granova_test.r

It'll run a bisect on ggplot2, marking any commits that successfully print the graph as good, and any that throw an error as bad. It ended up with this result:
===========
6ba21aee4e99f6c1888d7c8732bbf5257749b160 is the first bad commit
commit 6ba21aee4e99f6c1888d7c8732bbf5257749b160
Author: hadley <h.wi...@gmail.com>
Date:   Fri May 20 07:35:40 2011 -0500

    Convert coord to S3
===========

You can view the changes made in this commit with:
  git diff 6ba21 6ba21^
... or of course you can look at it on Github

Once you're all done with this, make sure to re-install whatever version of ggplot2 you were using before.

I find it pretty amazing that, even though I know almost nothing about your problem, the script can track down where it came from.

-Winston

You can also look at str(this) and str(list(...)). Anyway, it's somewhere within this function is where it dies. (And it looks like this function is in geom_rug_alt.r.)

If you exit to the browser selection thing again by pressing 'c' or just Enter, then you can go into 20, which is this function. Once you're in there, you can look around with ls() and other commands like that.

>From a little exploration, it looks like it's dying on the second line:
data <- coordinates$transform(data, scales)

The problem is that coordinates$transform is NULL. That syntax, obj$blah, is the syntax used by proto. But, as noted in my other email, the commit that broke everything is the one where coord was converted from proto to S3.

If you take a look at the new version of geom-rug.r, you'll see the new syntax is:
data <- coord_transform(coordinates, data, scales)

You may want to examine the new geom-rug.r and see if there are any other changes that you need to copy over to geom_rug_alt.r.

Good luck!

messages.subject: Re: Updated version of 0.9.0 transition guide
messages.body_plain:
Dennis,

First, I want to say thanks for the fantastic work you've put into this transition guide. It really nicely outlines some of the core new features of the package, and I appreciate everyone's contributions to it.

I have a suggestion about your section on "guides(): include a table of the arguments guides() can take. As a newcomer to ggplot2 0.9.0, I'm unfamiliar with all of the options one can pass to guides. A really helpful addition to your transition guide would be a table that outlines all of the parameters one could pass to guides(). I might take Hadley's web-based documentation for the Aesthetics section of common geoms <http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_point.html> as a starting point.

I raise this issue for three reasons:
>From the transition guide itself it's not clear what the total set of options are that one could pass to guides
The help file for guides() within R doesn't provide a comprehensive set of options either, nor does it have a "see also" link to any page that might.
Combining 1 and 2, how are new users going to learn all of the arguments that guides() takes? That's the problem I'm having: no reference that I know of contains them all.
Again, I think the ggplot2 transition guide you've created is really a great and helpful document. I'm just hoping we can extend it (and ggplot2's in-R documentation) to make clear what guides() can do.

- B

messages.body_plain:
Hi dear all,

I have been working with ggplot2 0.9 recently and hope to catch up and
get my package ready when ggplot2 is released on March 1st.

I noticed there is a autoplot s3 generic function defined inside
ggplot2 (0.9), which is function

>autoplot
function(x, ...) {
 UseMethod("autoplot")
}

so inside my own package, I could just setGeneric("autoplot") and
define other S4 methods to dispatch autoplot on different S4 classes.

Is it possible or does it make sense to change the signature "x" to
more general "object" or "data"?  in my case, I hope to dispatch
different method on "object" and reserve the argument name "x" to
specify the x variable, "x" is kind of special for generic plot
function. And I an not sure if it's a good practice  redefine the
generic inside my package or not, like

setGeneric("autoplot", function(object, ...)
standardGeneric("autoplot"))

it probably work inside my package, but if users want to use ggplot2
functionality, they will load ggplot2 and I believe it will override
the generic defined inside my own package?

or is there any other work around I could reserve "x" and use
different name "object" for dispatching?

Thanks

Tengfei

messages.subject: Re: Issues and pull requests
messages.body_plain:
Brian and Winston,

The Github conceptual model for a Pull Request seems to be "Issue + Code": https://github.com/blog/712-pull-requests-2-0

I think the "fixes #xx" or "references #xx" is itself a suitable work-around. I guess my question is:
If there's already a documented issue, and
Someone else already has a pull request outstanding, then
Why would a user submit a (competing?) pull request instead of commenting on the existing request?
I suppose if you really thought you could design a better patch than is in the existing pull, it's worth submitting your own pull request. But if you did submit a competing patch I'd still think a "references #xx" where xx is either an issue number or a pull request makes sense. The advantage to each request generating a new issue number is that it allows for separation of code and issues, as well as unique referencing.

Winston notes:

> For one bug, I'm currently on my third attempt (and pull request)! This may cause some problems when attaching a pull request to an existing issue. Then again, I guess it's possible in these cases to close the old issue and create a new pull request that references the old issue.

I think that's exactly right: if you're revising a pull request substantially then create a new request and close the original. I've submitted a pull request, been asked to rebase, and thus closed the original and resubmitted a new request. To me, that's a totally sensible model, but I'm interested in your thoughts.

- B

messages.subject: Another(!) update of the transition guide
messages.subject_clean: Another(!) update of the transition guide
messages.body_plain:
Greetings all:

Another iteration of the transition guide is submitted for your
approval. The base font has been changed to Charter (in the mathdesign
package), which is part of the MiKTeX-2.9 distribution and AFAIK the
TeXLive distribution, but it's not too difficult to modify if
necessary. The TOC is now two columns in a Helvetica font, using the
multitoc package in LaTeX. I also changed to double quotes in the code
because straight quotes are easier to read in code than curly ones.

The major set of changes, due to a request by Brian Danielak, occurs
in the section on guides. Tables of the arguments common to both
functions, as well as those specific to one of them, are included, as
well as an expanded discussion about how to call the guide functions.
Let me know if that works (or not).

The included pdf is set up for color highlighting with color graphics,
some of which may not show up particularly well on a B/W printer. In
the previous update, I pushed separate versions for color and B/W
printing to GitHub; in this update, there will only be one .Rnw file
which uses conditional evaluation to toggle color or black and white

messages.subject: Git submodules
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

I recently issued a pull request for a bug fix which also requires a change to the scales package. If someone tries to use the changed version of ggplot2 without installing the changed version of scales, it will break completely -- I don't think it would be possible at all to make a graph with a discrete scale.

As things get spun off into smaller packages, this sort of problem will happen more and more. I believe that git submodules are the way to handle this issue of synchronization between packages. I'd like to suggest that ggplot2 add scales, plyr and whatever else it needs (at least from Hadley's set of packages) as submodules.

I don't have any experience working with submodules, but I believe this means that:
- When someone clones ggplot2, they also get a clone of scales.
- Each commit of ggplot2 also references a particular commit of the submodule.
- This doesn't require any changes to the scales project on github. If another package uses scales as a submodule, that has no impact on the main scales project.

With a submodule, every commit in ggplot2 will be a snapshot of ggplot2 and the environment it depends on. In my recent adventures with bisect tests, I keep running into a block of about 40 commits that can't even be loaded, and I suspect it has something to do with some dependencies that are different now than they were at the time those commits were made. (A lot of bugs seem to be in this untestable range!) Submodules should be able to freeze all these things together in each commit.

If anyone here has experience with git submodules, it would be great to hear if you think they will solve these issues and work the way I've described.

http://help.github.com/submodules/
http://book.git-scm.com/5_submodules.html

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: dotplot point shapes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I had another look at the imaginative constants defining the point
shape sizes. As best as I could work out, the scaling factors for the
relevant shapes (fill and col) look like this,

fullSymbols <- function(type=c("round", "square", "diamond",
"utriangle", "dtriangle"),
                        size=unit(3, "cm"), ...){

  type <- match.arg(type)
  scaling <- switch(type,
                    "round" = 4/3,
                    "square" = 10 * par("cin")[1],
                    "diamond" = 10 * par("cin")[1] / sqrt(2),
                    "utriangle" = 1,
                    "dtriangle" = 1)

  pch <- switch(type,
                "round" = 21,
                "square" = 22,
                "diamond" = 23,
                "utriangle" = 24,
                "dtriangle" = 25)

  g <- pointsGrob(pch=pch, size=scaling*size, default.units="npc",
                  gp=gpar(col="red", fill="blue", alpha=0.5, lwd=20),
x=0.5,y=0.5,...)
  b <- rectGrob(x=0.5,y=0.5, width=size, height=size,
                gp=gpar(lty=2, fill=NA, col="black")) # snug box to size

  gTree(children=gList(g, b))
}

grid.newpage()
library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(
             fullSymbols("round"),
             fullSymbols("square"),
             fullSymbols("diamond"),
             fullSymbols("utriangle"),
             fullSymbols("dtriangle"))

and the last two presumably require some offset as well.

I don't know if it's useful, but if people have started mapping
colour, then I'm guessing shape might be desirable too (if only for
black and white prints).

Cheers,

b.

>
> I recently issued a pull request for a bug fix which also requires a change to the scales package. If someone tries to use the changed version of ggplot2 without installing the changed version of scales, it will break completely -- I don't think it would be possible at all to make a graph with a discrete scale.
>

I'd like to suggest that ggplot2 add scales, plyr and whatever else it needs (at least from Hadley's set of packages) as submodules.
>
> I don't have any experience working with submodules, but I believe this means that:
> - When someone clones ggplot2, they also get a clone of scales.
> - Each commit of ggplot2 also references a particular commit of the submodule.
> - This doesn't require any changes to the scales project on github. If another package uses scales as a submodule, that has no impact on the main scales project.
>
> With a submodule, every commit in ggplot2 will be a snapshot of ggplot2 and the environment it depends on. In my recent adventures with bisect tests, I keep running into a block of about 40 commits that can't even be loaded, and I suspect it has something to do with some dependencies that are different now than they were at the time those commits were made. (A lot of bugs seem to be in this untestable range!) Submodules should be able to freeze all these things together in each commit.
>
> If anyone here has experience with git submodules, it would be great to hear if you think they will solve these issues and work the way I've described.

I've a bit of experience with submodules. My point of view is that they are useful but tricky.

In the case of ggplot, because of the issue of version synchronization that you mention, I actually created a meta-repository which holds the repositories of the packages that ggplot uses:
	https://github.com/jiho/ggplot2-workspace
This repository is only submodules and a few scripts. It has to work this way because submodules need to be in a subdirectory of the main repo, so scales cannot be a submodule of ggplot, because this would create a "scales" subdirectory inside ggplot architecture which would probably mess things up.

I could add plyr (and probably remove roxygen now) and update everything etc. I just let this sit since June.

The reason its tricky is this:
- you clone the meta-repo (ggplot2-workspace); what you have at this point is just pointers towards a given commit for each submodule
- you "initiate" all submodules; now you have all the code in all subdirectories
- you work in ggplot2 and scales and create commits; this changes the head commit and the pointers are not up to date anymore
- you go back to the meta-repo and commit+push the changes to the pointers so that everything is compatible between all modules

Now if somebody else clones the meta repo, the problem is that it has pointers towards commits that don't exist because you didn't push the commits to ggplot2 and scales. There is now way but discipline around this: you have to push what's inside the submodule *before* doing anything in the meta-repo.
And the problem with this of course is that not everyone can push to ggplot2's main repo. With the current system of pull request etc. the best workable solution I can think of is:

# get the meta-repo
git clone g...@github.com:jiho/ggplot2-workspace.git
cd ggplot2-workspace

# initiate modules
git submodule init
git submodule update

# get to work inside ggplot2
cd ggplot2
git branch myBranch
git checkout myBranch

# work, work, work

# now put those changes online
# - fork ggplot on github
# - add your fork as a remote
git remote add myFork https://github.com/your-name/ggplot2
# - push your branch there
git push myFork myBranch

# do the same with scales
cd ../scales
git branch myBranch
git checkout myBranch
# work, work, work
git remote add myFork https://github.com/your-name/scales
git push myFork myBranch

# Now:
# - create a pull request between Hadley's ggplot master and your myBranch branch
# - create a pull request between Hadley's scales master and your myBranch branch
# In both refer to the other pull request so that Hadley knows to include both of them at the same time.

# Hadley then does
git clone g...@github.com:jiho/ggplot2-workspace.git
cd ggplot2-workspace
cd ggplot2
# include the pull request
git pull/push
cd ../scales
# include the pull request
git pull/push
cd ..
git commit -m "Include work by … in pull requests ## and ##" ggplot2 scales
git push

# Now ggplot2, scales, and the meta-repo are up to date and point to the same commits. If you want to use this "certified" version on your machine you do
cd ggplot2-workspace
cd ggplot2
git checkout master
cd ../scales
git checkout master
cd ..
git submodule update
# this would fetch the correct commits in ggplot2 and scales, even if they are not the HEAD of the master branch.

You can see how cumbersome that is and how it adds work to Hadley's already busy schedule (which is the reason why my meta-repo is just sitting there since June). But, again, I cannot think of another way to use submodules as a way to ensure version compatibility. I think they are mostly designed to allow to use libraries within a main project.

I would love to be proved wrong.

Jean-Olivier Irisson

My worry would be that releasing packages becomes tricky. If ggplot2 and scales become intimately tied to one another with cross-dependencies, won't new versions of the packages (in this case scaled and ggplot2) have to be released at exactly the same time? That's essentially isomorphic to the problem Hadley's experienced already with ggplot2 v0.9.0. That is:
Because of the internal changes to ggplot2, I think not all developers could make their packages compatible with BOTH 0.8.9 and 0.9.0. I'm pretty sure I can, but I don't expect everyone else can.
That means their newest packages break if CRAN doesn't have 0.9.0, and their old ones break if CRAN has the latest ggplot2.
Which results in the weird situation of feeling like 0.9.0 and all its 0.9.0-only compatible dependencies need to be released at the same time on CRAN
It seems to me that using submodules alone would perpetuate that problem internally amongst the ggplot2, scales, and other packages.

messages.body_plain:
On 2012-Feb-08, at 17:24 , Tengfei Yin wrote:
>
> I am thinking, model and other arguments could always be passed in your s3 or s4 autoplot function, it's just I really don't feel comfortable with "x" being the generic arguments.
>
> Since fortify() is also generic function, and I assume it has the same meaning of "data", with the one in autoplot or ggplot, it means just "original data",

No, `data` in fortify is indeed original data but not equivalent to what is given to autoplot. I expect to be able to give to autoplot an object (any object, not necessarily a data.frame) and possibly the original data, and have autoplot do something "clever" with it.

If the autoplot generic is

autoplot <- function(data, ...) {
	UseMethod("autoplot")
}

then a method using fortify would be

autoplot.myClass <- function(data, …) {

	d <- fortify(model=data, …)
	…
}

which is confusing at best. In addition, it prevent passing a data argument to fortify through `…`.

> it could also be defined in several different way and dispatch on signature "data" and "model" as user's need.

I'm afraid I don't understand this :-/

> "model" for me is more like a "modelling" results like from lm or somethings, not as "original object"  we expect in autoplot generic.

Indeed `model` is a bit specific, hence my suggestion to use `object`. However, I don't think autoplot should only receive the original data. I fully expect to be able to do

m <- lm(y~x, data=d)
autoplot(m)

Overall, I really think that x was better than data but that object would be better than x.

Font sizes in geom_text/annotate seem to be very different from those in theme_text. In this example, both sizes are set to 12, but the result is very different:

ggplot(data.frame(x=1:3), aes(x=x, y=x)) + geom_point() +

In the code for geom_text, the textGrob gets this, with units="native":
  fontsize = size * .pt,

In theme_text, the textGrob gets this, with units="npc":
 fontsize = size

.pt is defined in aaa-constants.r to be:
.pt <- 1 / 0.352777778

Anyone know why it's like this?

-Winston

Could this be included in ggplot2? In fact, since scale_x_log10() now
appears a little redundant, given the more general
scale_continuous(trans=""), could we make it a convenience function
that selects either style?

scale_x_log10 <- function(..., style=c("original", "transformed")) {

  style <- match.arg(style)

  breaks <- switch(style, "original"=NULL,
"transformed"=trans_breaks(’log10’, function(x) 10^x))
  labels <- switch(style, "original"=NULL,
"transformed"=trans_format(’log10’, math_format(10^.x)))
  dots <- list(...)

  params <-  modifyList(dots, list(trans = log10_trans(),
breaks=breaks, labels=labels))
  do.call(scale_x_continuous, params)

}

set.seed(123)
DF <- data.frame(x = rlnorm(1000, m = 1, sd = 0.2), y=rnorm(1000))

p <- ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y=y)) + geom_point()

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(
p + scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10"),
p + scale_x_log10(style="original"), # equivalent to the previous one
p + scale_x_log10(style="transformed")) # old style

In all of the above the minor_breaks are in the midposition between
breaks; in fact I was not successful in changing them at all with

minor_breaks=trans_breaks("log10", function(x) 10^x, n=100)

(first few graphs anyway): http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-log_plot

1                        10                      100                    1000

messages.subject: Re: Git submodules
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Feb 8, 2012 at 6:54 AM, Jean-Olivier Irisson <iri...@normalesup.org> wrote:
> I've a bit of experience with submodules. My point of view is that they are useful but tricky.
>
> In the case of ggplot, because of the issue of version synchronization that you mention, I actually created a meta-repository which holds the repositories of the packages that ggplot uses:
>        https://github.com/jiho/ggplot2-workspace
> This repository is only submodules and a few scripts. It has to work this way because submodules need to be in a subdirectory of the main repo, so scales cannot be a submodule of ggplot, because this would create a "scales" subdirectory inside ggplot architecture which would probably mess things up.

I just tried adding scales as a submodule, under ggplot2/deps/scales, and it didn't seem to be a problem for R CMD check.

Jean-Olivier, I think it's actually not necessary to have a meta repo... This is long, but I think it should help clear things up.

I added scales as a submodule to my local ggplot2 repo (actually, a copy of my ggplot2 repo). This only needs to be the person who adds it as a submodule -- me, in this test case:
  git clone g...@github.com:USERNAME/ggplot2.git
  cd ggplot2
  git submodule add g...@github.com:hadley/scales.git deps/scales

Then each new commit in my ggplot2 repo references the current commit in the deps/scales repo. If any new commits show up in deps/scales, ggplot2 will know about it and reference the current commit.

Here's the bit that I think is important:
- The /ggplot2/deps/scales repo should be essentially read-only most of the time -- it is used ONLY to pull from the main scales repo.
- It won't automatically pull the changes from the main scales repo. So even if there's active development going on the main scales repo, that won't affect the state of the /ggplot2/deps/scales submodule, until someone tells it to.
- If you want to work on scales, you should should work on a different copy of the scales repo.

To see what it's like to work with from the "client developer" side, clone my submodule test repo:
  git clone g...@github.com:wch/ggplot2-smtest.git
  cd ggplot2-smtest

If you look in deps/scales/, you'll see nothing there. And if you plan on never working on scales, that's fine. Each commit in the ggplot2-smtest repo references a commit in deps/scales, but that doesn't mean that every developer needs to have a copy of scales. In the ggplot2 commit, it'll add a reference to the current commit in deps/scales/:
  79603ba9706f0698191dc4ed38973b98bc4cb262 deps/scales
That's all that most people will get, and all that they'll need.

If you do want to get a copy of the submodules, run:

  git submodule init
  git submodule update

This will clone the remote repo github.com/hadley/scales <http://github.com/hadley/scales> into deps/scales. It uses Hadley's repo because when I set up the submodule, I pointed to that repo. If you want to keep your submodule up-to-date with the commit referenced by ggplot2, you'll have to occasionally run 'git submodule update'. (Note that this does _not_ keep it up-to-date with the main scales repo!)

In summary, from the typical developer's point of view, there's no more complexity to using ggplot2 with submodules, because they can just ignore them. The key is that you never work on the submodule -- if you want to work on it, use a different copy of the repo. The advantage to this system is that each commit of ggplot2 will point to a particular commit of the submodules, so if you have to check out an old ggplot2 commit, you can get the state of its dependencies at the time of that commit. For example, if ggplot2 had a plyr submodule, the commit of ggplot2 tagged 0.9.0 could have pointed to the plyr commit with tag 1.7.

Now, there is complexity if you want to make changes synchronously in the two repos. It's not super difficult -- you just have to make sure that everyone has access to the new commits in the submodule before (or at the same time) that they have access to new commits in the ggplot2 repo. Otherwise they may be unable to update their submodule to keep current with the main repo. But I think cases like this will be rare, and worth the trouble -- it's better than just having two completely unsynchronized projects

A couple more things about my ggplot2-smtest repo: There are two commits that I added: the first commit added the deps/scales submodule (with a slightly old state, a few commits behind 'master' in the main shared repo), and the second commit updated deps/scales to the present state of 'master' in the main repo. As I said earlier, if you like, you can ignore the submodule altogether, and work on ggplot2-smtest like normal. You can even submit pull requests to me. What you shouldn't do is work on deps/scales.

-Winston

will not be a part of panel gtalbe (like position = c(x, y) in

of course, this idea will be improved.

messages.subject: Re: dotplot point shapes
messages.body_plain:
I think the idea is to fit them into the bounding box. It's critical that they all have the same width, because dot width represents bin width. Also, it's important that they each have the same height, so that for any number of dots, they stack to the same height (useful for comparing groups).

I think the square doesn't work, since the stacked points would be indistinguishable. The triangles should be usable. They don't have to fit exactly into the bounding box. If they're a little smaller, I think that's OK. The triangles would look a little strange when stacking along the x axis instead of y. It would probably be a good idea to rotate them in that case.

Baptiste - thanks for figuring out the scaling ratios!

-Winston

messages.subject: geom_text rendering
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm in the process of updating my package (Deducer) to ggplot2 0.9,
and I'm checking my plotting functions to make sure that nothing
untoward has happened to them. I have a function that creates a roc
plot:

rocplot<-
function(logistic.model,diag=TRUE,pred.prob.labels=FALSE,prob.label.digits=3,AUC=TRUE)
{
	##Adapted from lroc in epicalc
	firsttable <- table(logistic.model$fitted.values, logistic.model$y)
	colnames(firsttable) <- c("Non-diseased", "Diseased")
	firsttable1 <- cbind(as.numeric(rownames(firsttable)), firsttable)
	rownames(firsttable1) <- rep("", nrow(firsttable1))
	colnames(firsttable1)[1] <- "predicted.prob"
	secondtable <- firsttable
	for (i in 1:length(secondtable[, 1])) {
		secondtable[i, 1] <- (sum(firsttable[, 1]) - sum(firsttable[(1:i),
									1]))/sum(firsttable[, 1])
		secondtable[i, 2] <- (sum(firsttable[, 2]) - sum(firsttable[(1:i),
									2]))/sum(firsttable[, 2])
		rownames(secondtable)[i] <- rownames(secondtable)[i]
	}
	secondtable <- as.data.frame(rbind((c(1, 1)), secondtable))
	colnames(secondtable) <- c("Spec", "Sens")
	model.des <- paste("logit (", deparse(logistic.model$formula),
			")", sep = "")
	auc <- 0
	for (i in 1:(nrow(secondtable) - 1)) {
		auc <- auc + (secondtable[i, 1] - secondtable[(i + 1),
							1]) * 0.5 * (secondtable[i, 2] + secondtable[(i +
										1), 2])
	}

	p<-qplot(Spec, Sens,data=secondtable[nrow(secondtable):1,], xlab = "1-
Specificity",
			ylab = "Sensitivity",main=model.des, xlim = (c(0, 1)), ylim = (c(0,
1)))+geom_step()
	if(diag)
		p<-p+geom_segment(aes(x=0,y=0),xend=1,yend=1,colour="red",size=1.5)
	if(pred.prob.labels)
		p<-p+geom_text(size=3,angle=-45,aes(x=Spec+.03,y=Sens-.03,

label=formatC(as.numeric(rownames(secondtable)),digits=prob.label.digits)))
	if(AUC)
		p<-p+geom_text(aes(x=.
8,y=0.05,label=paste("AUC=",formatC(auc,digits=4))))
	p
}

It can be run with something like:

model.glm <- glm(formula=income>5930.5 ~ education + women +
type,family=binomial(),data=Prestige,na.action=na.omit)
rocplot(model.glm)

On my system, the label "AUC=0.9342" is rendered very poorly. I
checked it with pdf and JavaGD devices, and both had the same
rendering. Any thoughts?

Best,
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The comment " label "AUC=0.9342" is rendered very poorly." would
suggest that the geom_text is overlaid multiple times. This is a
common issue, when the global mapping of the plot interferes with the
layer. One way around it is to explicitly pass a data argument,

geom_text(aes(x=x,y=y,label=label), data =
data.frame(x=.8,y=0.05,label=paste("AUC=",formatC(auc,digits=4))))

there used to be .inherit.aes=FALSE to that effect too, but I cannot
see it working here.

HTH,

b.

messages.subject: Re: Error installing ggplot2 0.9.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You need dev_mode() to be ON in order to install development versions
of R packages. You should also have Rtools installed, although I don't
think it's strictly necessary for compiling ggplot2 since it is pure
R. You should do this:

library('devtools')
dev_mode()   # should reply dev mode: ON
install_github('ggplot2')

You don't get a traceback because the R function returned no error; it
was the compilation that failed.

When I load up devtools, I get the message
"Rtools not in path, adding automatically."
I don't know if this is platform specific or not because I've only
done it in Windows 7. At the very least, the message tells you that
Rtools is installed on your system.

However, you *do* need to have dev_mode ON before installing ggplot2
or any other package from GitHub.

Here's an example from loading the development version of the ggmap
package this morning:

> library('devtools')
Rtools not in path, adding automatically.
> dev_mode()
Dev mode: ON
> install_github('ggmap', username = 'dkahle')
Installing ggmap from dkahle
Installing ggmap

Dennis

Actually, I ended up solving this problem by doing the following:

> tar -czf ggplot2_0.9.0.tar.gz hadley-ggplot2-89906e6/

after that, in R,
> install_github('ggplot2', username='hadley')
succeeded.

The obscure directory I got directly from the error message.
I guess however it (install_github?) was unzipping the downloaded package, the package is getting deleted on my system, but not on others who haven't been having issues. If anyone else is having the same issue on Mac OS X Lion, I guess this might be worth a try.

Thanks all!

messages.subject: Re: Transition guide from 0.8.9 to 0.9.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dennis,

Awesome job, thanks!
Looking at the code I have a couple of suggestions:

- use the jpeg package to read Hadley's picture. It's probably easier
to install than ReadImages (no system dependency).
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/jpeg/index.html
The function is called readJPG()

- the R script file looks like it was manually put together. I think
you have two options that might be useful (especially for updates):
tangle from the knitr document (use purl('guide.Rnw') instead of
knit('guide.Rnw')), or use the externalization of code chunks
(http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/) where you put
references ##@knitr chunk1 in an external R file, and call them by
name <<chunk1>>@ in the .Rnw document.

- use an incremental, unique indicator for each new plot, e.g. p1, p2,
p3, p4, ... (at least for the major specimen) so that we can refer to
a specific plot in the absence of figure captions in the document.

- the R logo is stretched; perhaps it's a good place to use

messages.subject: over-clipping in ggplot2 layout
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I haven't seen this issue raised, but maybe I missed it. If you look
at the legend of the last plot in page 8 of the transition guide,
you'll see that the legend is clipped. I ran into this same issue
yesterday with a legend.position="top", legend.direction="horizontal"
and many labels. It seems the new layout based on gtable is clipping
these "annotations" to the width and height of the plot panel, where
it could be argued that they shouldn't be clipped at all (to avoid the
risk of masking information).

I can produce a minimal example and file an issue if it hasn't been
discussed already.

Cheers,
b.

Hi dev members,

Here is an initial implementation of the next version of position guide.

x <- seq(0, 10, 0.1)
y <- sin(x * pi)

qplot(x, y, geom = "line") +
  scale_x_continuous(guide = guide_axis(position = "top")) +
  scale_y_continuous(guide = guide_axis(position = "right"))

qplot(x, y, geom = "line") +
  scale_x_continuous(guide = guide_range(size = 1, label = "1 mm")) +
  scale_y_continuous(guide = guide_range(size = 0.5, label =
expression(paste(0.5, mu, "V")))) +
  opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(), panel.grid.minor = theme_blank())

qplot(x, y, geom = "line") +
  scale_x_continuous(guide = guide_range(size = 1, label = "1 mm",
position = c(0.1, 0.1))) +
  scale_y_continuous(guide = guide_range(size = 0.5, label =
expression(paste(0.5, mu, "V")))) +
  opts(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(), panel.grid.minor = theme_blank())

the images are attached.

some syntax suger like this will appear.

- Is this interface reasonable?

messages.subject: Plot Builder updated for ggplot2 0.9
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Good work with ggplot2 0.9.0. I have spent the last week and a half
updating the ggplot2 plot builder in Deducer to reflect these changes,
as well as a few unrelated improvements. I would appreciate commentary
and bug reports. Here are two videos to wet your appetite:

neolab.stat.ucla.edu/cranstats/deducer_ggplot2_090_1.mov <http://neolab.stat.ucla.edu/cranstats/deducer_ggplot2_090_1.mov>
neolab.stat.ucla.edu/cranstats/deducer_ggplot2_090_2.mov <http://neolab.stat.ucla.edu/cranstats/deducer_ggplot2_090_2.mov>

The Development version of Deducer can be installed with:

install.packages("Deducer")
Sys.setenv(NOAWT=1)
install.packages("Deducer",,"http://www.rforge.net",type="source")
Sys.unsetenv("NOAWT")

And you can download and launch the JGR console with:

Sys.setenv(NOAWT=1)
library(JGR)
Sys.unsetenv("NOAWT")
JGR()

More detailed information is available in the manual at deducer.org <http://deducer.org>.
Below are my notes as I was exploring the new version.

Best,
Ian

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 1 :

> ggplot() +
+ geom_point(aes(x = carat,y = price),data=diamonds) +
+ scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar_format())
Error in if (max(x) < 100) 2 else 0 :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

solution:

dollar_format <- function ()
{
    function(x) {
        x <- round_any(x, 0.01)
        nsmall <- if (max(x, na.rm=TRUE) < 100)
            2
        else 0
        str_c("$", format(x, nsmall = nsmall, trim = TRUE, big.mark = ","))
    }
}

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 2:

What is the avantage of not using trans_breaks/trans_format as a
default in the transforms scale_*_log10. Is scientific format ever
more readable than the nice exponential format?

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 3:

Should override.aes=list(alpha=1) be default if alpha is constant? Can
anyone think of a useful plot where alpha in the legend is desired?

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 4:

Should map_data have a try_require("maps") in it?

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 5:

Is it intended behavior that geom_map requires expand_limits in order
to be plotted correctly? It seems like a relatively minor change to
add the call to expand_limits internally.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 6:

Some thought seems to have gone into SpatialPolygonDataFrames visavi
the fortify methods. Wouldn't it be more elegant for geom_map to
operate directly on SpatialPolygonDataFrames objects passed through
the data parameter. This would eliminate the need to keep track of two
data objects, and the key between them (map_id).

So far as I can tell the easiest way to do this is to change ggplot2's
internal representation of "data" from data.frame to list. i.e.:

data <- c(data@data,..polygons..=polygons(data))

 I tried mucking around in the source code, but didn't have much success.
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 7:

treatment of NAs are handled by the scale, but they are not included
in the legend, leading to plotting elements which the reader has no
way of interpreting. My personal view is that NA should be excluded by
default.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 8:

What about a scale for rank transform?

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 9:

why is stat_ydensity not exported?

---------------------------------------------------------------------

Note 10:

in geom_dotplot, I seem to be getting more overlapping than I would
expect. How much overlapping should be apparent when looking at the
points with alpha=.5?

Because a huge number of people complained about the old format :/

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------

> Note 3:
>
> Should override.aes=list(alpha=1) be default if alpha is constant? Can
> anyone think of a useful plot where alpha in the legend is desired?

The principle is to always match the data, unless explicitly otherwise
stated.  I'm not sure if I want to make an exception for alpha, even
if it's useful.

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Note 4:
>
> Should map_data have a try_require("maps") in it?

Yes - added.

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Note 5:
>
> Is it intended behavior that geom_map requires expand_limits in order
> to be plotted correctly? It seems like a relatively minor change to
> add the call to expand_limits internally.

Yes - this is something I'd rather fix in the next version where geoms
will tell the scales what their physical dimension is.

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Note 6:
>
> Some thought seems to have gone into SpatialPolygonDataFrames visavi
> the fortify methods. Wouldn't it be more elegant for geom_map to
> operate directly on SpatialPolygonDataFrames objects passed through
> the data parameter. This would eliminate the need to keep track of two
> data objects, and the key between them (map_id).

That assumes that SpatialPolygonDataFrames is the most common map data
format.  I'm not sure it is - but you're right that that code would be
more efficient if it didn't have to coerce everything into a data
frame (a la annotate_raster)

> Note 7:
>
> treatment of NAs are handled by the scale, but they are not included
> in the legend, leading to plotting elements which the reader has no
> way of interpreting. My personal view is that NA should be excluded by
> default.

NAs should always appear in the legend.  If they don't it's a bug.
The principle is that missing data should never be dropped
automatically.

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Note 8:
>
> What about a scale for rank transform?

Not sure if/how this would work when you have data coming across
multiple layers.  But it seems like a reasonable idea.  Could you file
as an issue?

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Note 9:
>
> why is stat_ydensity not exported?

Ooops, fixed.

> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Note 10:
>
> in geom_dotplot, I seem to be getting more overlapping than I would
> expect. How much overlapping should be apparent when looking at the
> points with alpha=.5?

I'll let Winston handle that.

> Note 10:
>
> in geom_dotplot, I seem to be getting more overlapping than I would
> expect. How much overlapping should be apparent when looking at the
> points with alpha=.5?

It's hard to say without seeing an example with data, but I can think of a few possibilities.

The dots are drawn with a fill and a outline (controlled with 'colour'). I added the outline because if you use just a fill, the result is jagged on a number of bitmap devices -- we've probably all seen this with geom_point. If you're using small points, the result is that the outline can make the entire dot slightly larger, leading to overlap. You can make the outline go away with colour=NA.

The other reason has to do with the way binning works. If you use geom_dotplot(binmethod="histodot"). But if you use the default "dotdensity" method, it can result in a fair bit of overlap, up to 1/2 the dot diameter. I've attached an example with values c(0.49, 1.4, 1.45, 1.5, 3, 4), and binwidth=1. The vertical lines mark where each data point is. The output in this case is not a great representation of the data, but this is the result of the binning algorithm from Wilkinson's dot plot paper.

In that paper, he describes a smoothing algorithm which can help reduce left-right bias (and possibly overlap). I made an attempt at implementing it, but either I didn't understand it, or there was an error in the description of the method. If someone would like to enlighten me, the paper is here:
www.cs.uic.edu/~wilkinson/Publications/dots.pdf <http://www.cs.uic.edu/~wilkinson/Publications/dots.pdf>

-Winston

This looks very cool... I have some questions and suggestions:

- Is it possible to have both the axis guide and the range guide?

- I assume that 'size' is the length of the line, in the data space. For consistency, you may want to use 'size' for the line thickness, and 'length' for the length.

- It looks like positioning is done panel's coordinate space, which goes from 0 to 1 on each axis. It may also be useful to be able to control the position in the data space. For example, you might want the guide to start at the 0 point of your data. I think this would also be useful when the guide is placed outside the plotting region.

- Is it possible to control the amount of space allocated for the guide_range? The x axis label is very far away from the plotting area, and bringing it closer would look better.

- I don't know if this is worth the trouble, but it would also be nice to have a dual-scale guide. If you look at Google maps, it shows the length for both km and miles, with one on top of the line and one on the bottom. (This would also require end markers for the lines)

- Is there a way to control the line ends? I think it would be useful to have the option of having flat ends (like error bars), and ones that are on one side only, as in Google maps (mentioned above).

- It would be useful to put something like "minor ticks" on the range guide. For example, when you set size=1, you might also want tick marks every 0.2.

-Winston

p1 <- qplot(x, y, geom = "line") +

> don't understand why latitude and longitude aren't always the native

Which Latitude and longitude? It can vary depending on which geodetic
datum is used. For spatial data, the x and y coordinates have special
privilege that doesn't exist for non-spatial data. Further, it makes
sense to think about rows of data being fundamentally associated with
geometric features (lines/polygons). You don't have to use
Spatial*DataFrames, but if you design a data structure with the
previous two sentences in mind, you'll end up with something similar.

I haven't worked with Spatial*DataFrames super extensively, but I
don't share your view that they are needlessly complicated and
difficult to work with.

Regardless, I think that if you were to imagine the most elegant way
to express a choropleth plot in the grammar of graphics, it wouldn't
involve preprocessing into two separate data.frames and keeping track
a key between them as an aesthetic.

On Tue, Feb 21, 2012 at 12:42 PM, Ian Fellows <ifel...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Just to be clear, here is an example:
>
> pdf()
> ggplot() +
>        geom_dotplot(aes(x = women),data=Prestige,alpha = 0.5)
> dev.off()
>
> this uses all the default settings, but more than just the outline is
> overlapping. If the dotsize parameter is changed, then things start to
> get very crazy.

That's just the way the binning algorithm works. Each stack of dots is centered at mean(min(x), max(x)), where x is the set of data points for that stack. It's possible for them to overlap by up to 1/2 the diameter of the dots. If you really don't like the way it looks, you can use method="histodot", or a smaller value for dotsize.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
>
> I was thinking it would be nice if you could do something like:
>
> gf <- guide_axis(position = "right", transform = function(x) 9/5*x + 32)

Unfortunately we need inverse function of transform.
This is because,

1) transform the range of data space into new space by transform function.
2) pretty breaks on the new space -> new breaks.
3) new breaks are only used for label.
4) new breaks need to be placed on the data space. here the new space
need to be inv-transed into data space.

One way is to explicitly require the inverse function such as,
transform = ..., inverse = ...

but this may be quite tough for users.

Another way is to assume linear transform if the inverse is missing,
with explicit warning message.

This works the transform is linear, but will not for non-linear
transform, e.g., data is liner space and additional log-space axis is
shown by transform = function(x) log(x).

kohske

Hi again all,

Sorry for all the traffic. I've taken some time to refactor the
non-gui parts of my DeducerSpatial package into a new package
OpenStreetMap. It should be up on r-forge when they do their next
package builds. I've included an autoplot function which create a
bunch of annotation_rasters for each tile of the map. One thing I
noticed is that geom_map ignores the alpha aesthetic. Is this
intended?

If I'm not mistaken, the raster images look better in ggplot2 than in
base graphics. Is that just my mind playing tricks on me?

require(OpenStreetMaps)
require(maps)
require(ggplot2)
gpclibPermit()

#download maps
mp <- openmap(c(53.38332836757155,-130.517578125),
		c(15.792253570362446,-67.939453125),4,'osm')
mp_bing <- openmap(c(53.38332836757155,-130.517578125),
		c(15.792253570362446,-67.939453125),4,'bing')
states_map <- map_data("state")
crimes <- data.frame(state = tolower(rownames(USArrests)), USArrests)

#transform to mercator projection
states_map_merc <- as.data.frame(
		project_mercator(states_map$lat,states_map$long))
states_map_merc$region <- states_map$region
states_map_merc$group <- states_map$group

#plot
pdf()
p <- autoplot(mp,expand=FALSE) + geom_polygon(aes(x=x,y=y,group=group),
		data=states_map_merc,fill="black",colour="black",alpha=.1) + theme_bw()
print(p)
p <- autoplot(mp_bing) +
geom_map(aes(x=-10000000,y=4000000,map_id=state,fill=Murder),
		data=crimes,map=states_map_merc,alpha=.1)

messages.subject: Updating granovaGG for ggplot 0.9.0
messages.body_plain:
A quick overview of what I did <https://github.com/briandk/granovaGG/pull/139/commits> to make my package compatible with both 0.8.9 and 0.9.0:
Require R 2.14.0 or greater
Explicitly import all of my packages dependencies (instead of counting on ggplot2 to drag them into the global namespace)
Replace the "value" parameter with "values" in all of my color scale calls
use ggplot2:::Geom (instead of just Geom) in the call for my custom geom
For those interested, we accomplished the whole transition with a Github Pull Request <https://github.com/blog/712-pull-requests-2-0>, which you can view here <https://github.com/briandk/granovaGG/pull/139/commits>. Pull requests are a great way to generate discussions and get feedback and code reviews, even (and especially!) in your own projects.

Hope this helps, and please ask if you have any questions about pull requests.

- B

messages.subject: Handling R CMD check "no visible binding for global variable" errors
messages.subject_clean: Handling R CMD check "no visible binding for global variable" errors
messages.body_plain:
So, I have a bunch of ggplot2-based functions that are (and always have been) throwing R CMD check warnings. Here's an example of such a function

  JitteredResponsesByContrast <- function (data) {
    return(
      geom_point(
               aes(
                 x = x.values,
                 y = y.values
               ),
               data     = data,
               position = position_jitter(height = 0, width = GetDegreeOfJitter(jj))
      )
    )
  }

And the corresponding R CMD check warning:

granovagg.contr : JitteredResponsesByContrast: no visible binding for
  global variable ‘x.values’
granovagg.contr : JitteredResponsesByContrast: no visible binding for
  global variable ‘y.values’

The problem (which I think I understand now) is that x.values and y.values are variables defined in the data frame that gets handed in. That's *why* I'm using the data = argument to geom_point(). But, since R CMD check sees no obvious binding (they're not defined globally or even within the JitteredResponsesByContrast function), it panics.

Here are my questions:
do other people get these warnings?
Are the warnings fair, since I'm playing well within the rules of ggplot2 syntax?
How have people addressed this to get their packages to pass R CMD check without errors and warnings?
ggplot2 v0.8.9, for example, is on CRAN even though it has exactly these kinds of warnings: http://www.R-project.org/nosvn/R.check/r-patched-linux-ix86/ggplot2-00check.html

messages.subject: table grob
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm working on a new version of tableGrob. A prototype is here:
https://gist.github.com/1899720

Now I need to add decorations, row+col headers, support for tables
package, etc. but I think the basic design is sound. How should the
row/column headers (and their justification) work with respect to the
new axis guides in ggplot2? My thinking is that only the core of the
table should be aligned with the plot panel, typically, so I would
specify the table justification relative to the core only. The
optional row and column header(s) would extend from there, on the
sides.

Cheers,

b.

messages.subject: geom for log tick marks
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

I've written a geom for log tick marks. It's at:
  https://gist.github.com/1920696
If you want to try it out, you should be able to copy and paste it into your R session to set up the function -- it's written so that it doesn't have to be in the ggplot2 namespace. (Unfortunately it's not possible to source a gist directly, since gists are served via https.)

Here are some examples:
library(MASS)
p <- ggplot(Animals, aes(x=body, y=brain)) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = trans_breaks("log10", function(x) 10^x),
                labels = trans_format("log10", math_format(10^.x))) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = trans_breaks("log10", function(x) 10^x),
                labels = trans_format("log10", math_format(10^.x))) +
  theme_bw()

# Basic log ticks, on left and bottom
p + geom_logticks()

# Add on the left, right, top, bottom (default is left and bottom)
p + geom_logticks(sides="lrtb")

# Change the length of the ticks, and in different units
p + geom_logticks(sides="lrtb", shortlen=1, longlen=4, units="mm")

Some notes:
- It presently works if there is a transformed scale, or if the data is transformed before it's plotted. It doesn't work correctly with coord_trans.
# Works properly
ggplot(Animals, aes(x=log(body,10), y=log(brain,10))) + geom_point() +
  geom_logticks()
# Doesn't work:
ggplot(Animals, aes(x=body, y=brain)) + geom_point() + geom_logticks() +
  coord_trans(xtrans="log10", ytrans="log10")

- The sides that the tick marks appear on are specified with a string containing any of "lrtb", for left, right, top, bottom. I'm open to suggestions about better or more elegant ways of specifying sides.

- The length of the ticks can be set with 'shortlen' and 'longlen', along with 'units'. I would have preferred to specify them as unit objects, like `shortlen=unit(0.2, "cm")`, but if I had used this as the default value for the argument, it would require the user to load the grid package to use geom_logticks, even if they didn't modify the length.

- With log10 tick marks, ticks at each 1 and 5 are longer. To disable making the 5 tick longer, set 'midticks=FALSE'.

- The default base is 10. It's possible to change the base, but I don't know if it makes sense to have diminishing tick marks like this with, say, base-2 or base-e.

- I don't know where the geom belongs -- it doesn't seem to fit as part of the main ggplot2 package, since it's a bit of a hack, and hopefully won't be necessary in future versions of ggplot2.

Comments and suggestions are welcome.

-Winston

messages.subject: Dotplot, position="stack"
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The new geom_dotplot() is great and creating some wonderful graphs.

However, should the position attribute behave like the geom_histogram?

x <- rnorm(100)
group <-c(rep("A", 60), rep("B", 40))
data <- data.frame(x=x, group=group)

plot.hist_identity <- ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) + geom_histogram(position="identity", alpha=0.5)
plot.hist_stack <- ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) + geom_histogram(position="stack", alpha=0.5)
plot.dotplot_identity <- ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) + geom_dotplot(method="histodot", position="identity", alpha=0.5)
plot.dotplot_stack <- ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) + geom_dotplot(method="histodot", position="stack", alpha=0.5)

Currently position="stack" behaves like position="identity" (alpha set so that you can see the overplotting).

Best wishes and many thanks for such a great library,

Matthew

messages.subject: Re: Dotplot, position="stack"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matthew -

The way that geom_dotplot is implemented is a bit different, and position="stack" won't work.  Here's an attempt at explaining the root of the problem:

With geom_histogram, the bars are stacked by moving their y position so that the starting y position of one bar is the ending y position of the one below it. When you resize a graph to be taller, the bars will scale accordingly.

With geom_dotplot, the dots are always circular, so when you resize the graph to be taller, they can't be stretched vertically the way that histogram bars are.

For reasons related to this, each stack of dots is a single grob, which has a y position for the baseline. Unlike the bars in geom_histogram the dot stacks don't have a real y height, since the y height of each stack can't be determined (at least, not with the way that ggplot2 currently works). And because it doesn't have a y height, position="stack" won't work.

All that said, it may be possible add a hack to support position="stack". You're not the only person who has asked about it... if it's something that's a lot of people need, I can take a look into it.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Dotplot, position="stack"
messages.body_plain:
Well, it turns out it wasn't as ugly as I thought it would be. I haven't really tested it thoroughly, but it works with these examples:

set.seed(113)
x <- rnorm(100)
group <-c(rep("A", 40), rep("B", 60))
data <- data.frame(x=x, group=group)

# histodot, no stack
ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, method="histodot", alpha=0.5)

# histodot with stack
ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, method="histodot", position="stack", alpha=0.5)

# dotdensity with bins aligned across groups (binpositions="all"), no stack
ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, binpositions="all", alpha=0.5)

# dotdensity with bins aligned across groups (binpositions="all"), and stack
ggplot(aes(x=x, fill=group), data=data) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=.2, binpositions="all", position="stack", alpha=0.5)

Also it doesn't work for binaxis="y". This is because stacking normally goes up, but when binaxis="y", it should go right. This could be remedied by using a new argument besides position="stack".

Making the geom capture the position="stack" argument was probably the least elegant part of implemention, so I'd be happy to get rid of that code. The new argument could be "stackgroups". The drawback to adding a new parameter is that it adds nonstandard user-facing code, for an operation that already exists (at least when binaxis="x").

Installing via install_github may not work for you because of a bug in some versions of devtools. Normally you can do this:
  library(devtools)
  dev_mode()
  install_github('ggplot2', 'wch', 'experimental')
But there is a problem with some versions of devtools where it doesn't actually use the branch.

https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/commit/eea56f62e28e1013d836c740b41da543a5eb1240

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: positional guides
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have uploaded the initial implementation of position guide.
https://github.com/kohske/ggplot2/tree/feature/pguide

Now, it works only with facet-null.
At the moment, two type of guides, guide-axis and guide-range are implemented
* guide-axis can work with coord-cartesian, coord-flip, and coord-polar.
* guide-range can work only with coord-cartesian.

you can find the test codes at inst/tests/visual-position-guides.r
Please find the attached images of the example outputs.

Any comments and suggestions are welcome.

thanks,

kohske
